newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro currency doubters ignore reality - German MEP.
newsitem.headline: Euro currency doubters ignore reality - German MEP.

text.p: Those who oppose the Europe's planned single currency on grounds of national sovereignty ignore the lack of influence they have in a Bundesbank-dominated EU, a German member of the European Parliament said on Friday.

"There's already a single, central bank operating and it's a German instrument," Christian Democrat deputy Elmar Brok said, referring to the dominant role of Germany's independent central bank in shaping monetary policy across the 15-nation European Union.

"Monetary union is a way of making this instrument into a European one so that for the people, they will be getting back sovereignty which because of market forces has been taken away from them," he told a conference on the European Union's future structure.
The largely Euro-sceptic audience gave a warm reception to British Referendum Party leader Sir James Goldsmith, who likened German Chancellor Helmut Kohl to 19th century leader Otto von Bismarck.

"Chancellor Kohl has a personal mission in my view to become the Bismarck of Europe on a grand scale and not just in German areas," said Goldsmith, who wants British voters to decide whether to stay in the EU.
"I am deeply for Europe," he said. "But a Europe of strong and independent nations."
Brok criticised those in countries like Sweden and Britain who attacked a policy which many of their fellow citizens had previously supported as a way to bring the German bank to heel.

"There are certain countries which are being very critical of (the planned European single currency), but they were the ones who called for a European currency and a European central bank in the 1980s because they did not want their monetary policy conducted by the Bundesbank," he said.
British Conservative member of parliament and prominent Euro-sceptic Bill Cash called for a halt to the single currency project and to closer European union.
"Monetary union will bring further unemployment with it and indeed less democracy and more disorder," he said to cheers from some in the 500-strong audience, many of them Swedes.
Cash said the EU's negotiations on its future structure, conducted within the so-called inter-governmental conference (IGC), should take stock but not risks.

"We need to use the IGC as it was intended: to review the progress of the Union over the last 40 years and not to continue on the path towards more and more majority voting and less power and less of a role for independent nation states.
"We must bring the whole of the movement towards political and monetary union to a halt in the IGC and get that connection back between the elite and the electorate," he added.
